items.name: Pleiades
items.hook: The Seven Sisters: the most obvious star cluster in the sky.
items.story: About 444 light-years away, the Pleiades hold over 1,000 young stars, and six or seven are easy to see without a telescope. Its blue haze isn't leftover birth material; the cluster is passing through a dusty patch of space. In Japan it is called Subaru.

items.name: Hyades
items.hook: The nearest open cluster, about 153 light-years away.
items.story: The Hyades is the closest open cluster to the Sun, roughly 625 million years old. Bright Aldebaran looks like part of it but is actually much closer to us, at 65 light-years. Precise distances to the Hyades help astronomers calibrate the cosmic distance ladder.

items.name: Beehive Cluster (Praesepe)
items.hook: Galileo turned a fuzzy glow into 40 stars.
items.story: This cluster in Cancer lies about 610 light-years away and is around 600 to 700 million years old. In 1609 Galileo's telescope resolved it into 40 stars. In 2012 astronomers found two hot Jupiters here, the first planets found around Sun-like stars in star clusters.

items.name: Orion Nebula
items.hook: A star nursery you can see with your eyes.
items.story: Visible to the naked eye in Orion's sword, this nebula is about 1,270 light-years away and is the closest region of massive star formation to Earth. Hubble has spotted more than 150 protoplanetary disks here, which may be young solar systems still forming.

items.name: Crab Nebula
items.hook: Wreckage of a star that exploded in 1054.
items.story: The Crab Nebula is what remains of a bright supernova seen in AD 1054 and recorded by Chinese astronomers. At its heart is the Crab Pulsar, a neutron star that spins about 30 times every second. It lies roughly 6,500 light-years away.

items.name: Ring Nebula
items.hook: A dying star's glowing smoke ring.
items.story: About 2,570 light-years away in Lyra, this ring of glowing gas was blown off by a star near the end of its life. What's left at the center is a white dwarf. Charles Messier found it in 1779.

items.name: Dumbbell Nebula
items.hook: The first planetary nebula ever discovered.
items.story: Charles Messier discovered this cloud in Vulpecula in 1764, making it the first planetary nebula known. It lies about 1,360 light-years away, and its expanding gas suggests an age of roughly 9,800 years. A white dwarf at the center lights it up.

items.name: Eagle Nebula
items.type: Emission nebula (H II region) with open cluster
items.hook: Home of Hubble's famous Pillars of Creation.
items.story: About 5,700 light-years away in Serpens, the Eagle Nebula holds a young star cluster and several active star-forming regions. In 1995 Hubble photographed its towering gas columns, now known as the Pillars of Creation, where new stars are forming.

items.name: Lagoon Nebula
items.hook: A giant star-forming cloud faintly visible without a telescope.
items.story: This giant glowing cloud in Sagittarius is about 4,100 light-years away and spans about 110 by 50 light-years. It is one of only two star-forming nebulae faintly visible to the naked eye from mid-northern latitudes. Its central Hourglass region shows signs of stars being born.

items.name: Hercules Globular Cluster
items.hook: Humanity sent a radio message here in 1974.
items.story: Hundreds of thousands of stars crowd into this ball about 24,000 light-years away. Edmond Halley discovered it in 1714. In 1974, the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a coded message about humans, DNA, and Earth's location toward it.

items.name: Omega Centauri
items.hook: The Milky Way's biggest globular cluster, maybe a galaxy's core.
items.story: With about 10 million stars, Omega Centauri is the largest and most massive known globular cluster in the Milky Way. Ptolemy listed it as a single star. It may be the core of a dwarf galaxy swallowed by our galaxy, and a 2024 study reported possible evidence of a central black hole.

items.name: Messier 4 (Spider Globular Cluster)
items.hook: The closest globular cluster, hiding some of the galaxy's oldest stars.
items.story: About 6,000 light-years away near Antares, M4 is the closest globular cluster to the Solar System. Some of its white dwarfs are among the oldest known stars in our galaxy. It also hosts a pulsar system with a planet about 2.5 times Jupiter's mass.

items.name: Wild Duck Cluster
items.hook: A packed cluster shaped like a flock of flying ducks.
items.story: This cluster in Scutum, about 6,100 light-years away, is one of the richest and most compact open clusters known. Its brightest stars form a triangle that resembles a flying flock of ducks, which gives it its name. It is roughly 316 million years old.

items.name: Trifid Nebula
items.hook: Three kinds of nebula in one, split into three lobes.
items.story: About 4,100 light-years away in Sagittarius, the Trifid mixes a pink emission nebula, a blue reflection nebula, and dark dust lanes that split it into three lobes. It is a stellar nursery with about 3,100 young stars.

items.name: Andromeda Galaxy
items.type: Barred spiral galaxy (outside the Milky Way)
items.hook: A whole other galaxy you can see with your eyes.
items.story: Unlike everything else here, Andromeda lies outside the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light-years away, and holds roughly a trillion stars. It is visible to the naked eye on dark nights. It may one day collide with our galaxy, though newer Gaia-based studies make a merger look less likely.
